title: Treating Pupils as Capable Thinkers
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt argues that the books placed in pupils' hands are where a school's curriculum ambition becomes visible, so text choice is a curricular decision and not an afterthought. She asks teachers to test any text against a few questions: does its language give pupils something worth acquiring, does it open up a substantial idea, and does it reward a second look. Richness is not a matter of length, age or prizes, and a picture book or a well-chosen non-fiction piece can carry real intellectual weight. Myatt insists that weak decoders should not have their intellectual diet capped by their current decoding level, since read-aloud texts give them access to language they cannot yet manage alone. She also warns against smothering a good text with questions and vocabulary tasks before pupils have simply been absorbed in it. The piece closes by widening the lens from single books to the whole diet of reading across a term, year and key stage, and offers one practical starting point: ask of the latest class text, why this book, for these pupils, now?
points: Text choice is where curriculum vision turns into pupils' daily experience, so a school that claims an ambitious curriculum should be able to see that ambition in its books.
Judge a text by what it makes possible: acquirable language, a substantial idea, and enough depth to reward re-reading, not by length, age or awards.
Pupils who struggle to decode should still hear rich texts read aloud, because decoding proficiency should not set the ceiling on what they think about.
Give the first encounter with a rich text room to breathe before layering on questions, vocabulary work and curriculum links.
Audit the whole reading diet across a term, year and key stage rather than expecting any single book to do everything; start by asking why this book, for these pupils, at this point.
quotes: We can spend masses of time articulating a vision for reading and the curriculum, but the books we put into pupils’ hands are where that vision becomes visible. If we say every child deserves an ambitious curriculum, our text choices need to reflect that ambition.
Does its language give them something worth acquiring? Does it open up a substantial idea? Does it reward attention, offering more to notice when we return to it?

Richness does not depend on length; a picture book can carry considerable intellectual and emotional weight, just as a carefully chosen non-fiction text can prompt questions that take us well beyond the information on the page.
While their independent reading may need careful decoding support, the texts they hear read aloud can give them access to language and ideas they could not yet manage alone.
We should be very cautious about allowing a pupil’s current decoding proficiency to determine the limits of their intellectual experience.
The first encounter needs room to breathe. Pupils need the chance to become absorbed, to wonder what happens next, or simply to sit with something unexpected.
Choosing well also means looking beyond individual books to the diet of reading across a term, a year, and a key stage. No single text needs to do everything.
